bp: The ordinary problem behind this survey is simple: someone has a large image model that already learned broad visual patterns from massive image collections, and now they want to use it for a narrower image classification task. A hospital may need a scanner model, a retailer may need product categories, or a platform may need content labels. Rebuilding the whole model for every new task is expensive because the model contains many adjustable numbers, and full fine-tuning changes all of them. The paper asks how vision transformer models can be adapted without paying that full cost each time. Its object is not a new classifier but the design space of parameter-efficient fine-tuning for vision transformers: ways to keep most of the pretrained visual knowledge intact while changing only a small, carefully chosen part. The survey matters because practical deployment depends on the tradeoff among accuracy, memory, computation, and how easily the approach scales across many downstream tasks.
wh: The hard part is that a pretrained vision transformer is both useful and heavy. It is useful because large-scale pretraining has already taught it visual patterns that transfer to image classification tasks. It is heavy because full fine-tuning treats adaptation as if every internal setting might need to move, which raises computation and memory costs. A second difficulty is comparison. Parameter-efficient methods are not one trick with one cost. Additive methods attach small trainable pieces; reparameterization methods describe changes in a compact form; selective methods choose only some parts to update; hybrid methods combine choices; inference-efficient methods care about the cost when the model is used after training. These families trade accuracy, efficiency, and scalability differently. A method that saves training memory may add prediction-time overhead, while a method that is fast at prediction may be less flexible during adaptation. The survey is hard because it must organize this many-sided tradeoff, not merely rank techniques by one score.
naive: A smart beginner would take the pretrained vision transformer, copy it for the new image task, and train every adjustable number until the new labels are predicted well. That is full fine-tuning. It is attractive because it gives the model maximum freedom: any part of the visual pipeline can change if the new task needs it. The failure is cost and practicality. If every downstream task needs a separate fully changed copy, memory use grows quickly, training needs large hardware, and deployment becomes harder across many settings. The opposite naive shortcut is to freeze the model and only train a tiny final classifier. That saves cost, but it may not give the model enough room to adapt when the new images require different visual cues.
ap: The core idea of the survey is to treat efficient adaptation as a set of design choices about where change is allowed. Instead of asking whether to fine-tune or not, it asks which small part of the model should carry the task-specific information. In additive approaches, the base vision transformer is mostly preserved and small trainable components are inserted or attached. In reparameterization approaches, the change to the model is expressed through a smaller set of numbers rather than a full direct update. In selective approaches, only chosen layers or parameters are opened for training. Hybrid approaches mix these strategies when one kind of restriction is too narrow. Inference-efficient methods add another lens: they ask not only how cheap training is, but how costly the adapted model is when it classifies images later. The paper's central move is a taxonomy that turns a scattered method landscape into comparable mechanical families.
mech: The mechanism described by the survey runs as an organizing pipeline rather than as one experimental algorithm. The input is a collection of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods for vision transformers used in image classification. Each method starts from the same broad situation: a pretrained visual model has many internal settings, and a downstream task supplies labeled images that require adaptation. The survey then asks a concrete question of each method: where does the new task information enter the model, and what cost does that choice create? If the method is additive, the changed information sits in extra trainable pieces while the original model mostly stays fixed. If it is reparameterization-based, the method does not store a full free-form change; it stores a compact recipe that produces the needed adjustment. If it is selective, the method chooses a subset of the existing model to update and keeps the rest unchanged. If it is hybrid, it combines two or more of these routes. If it is inference-efficient, it is judged partly by what happens when the model is actually used for prediction. After sorting methods this way, the survey compares their design principles, strengths, limitations, evaluation protocols, and reported results. The output is not a single trained model but a map: for each family, what is saved, what flexibility is lost, and which accuracy-efficiency-scalability tradeoff the method is trying to occupy.
math: The main mathematical idea is constrained learning: instead of letting every adjustable number in the model move, the method restricts the search to a smaller set of changes. Learning from examples means defining what counts as a wrong image classification and adjusting allowed settings to reduce that wrongness. Full fine-tuning gives the search many degrees of freedom, which can fit the new task but costs memory and computation. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning deliberately shrinks the set of allowed moves. Additive methods create a small side path whose settings can change while the main path remains stable. Reparameterization methods say that a large possible change can be described through a smaller recipe, so the system searches over the recipe rather than every individual setting. Selective methods choose a few existing locations where movement is most likely to matter. Hybrid methods combine restrictions when one restriction alone gives too little room. The underlying tradeoff is compression versus flexibility: a smaller trainable part is cheaper and easier to store, but it may not express every change the task needs. The survey also uses comparison as a mathematical act: methods are judged by several quantities at once, including accuracy, memory, computation, prediction cost, and scalability. No single number can capture all of these, so the taxonomy is a way to make the tradeoffs visible.
dots: This paper sits in the conference's broader efficiency and scalability family. It shares a pressure with edge video adaptation, sparse recommendation representations, distributed parameter-efficient tuning, and privacy-friendly transformer adaptation: large pretrained models are useful, but moving or changing all of their internal state is too expensive for repeated deployment. It also connects to optimization, because every adaptation method must decide what kind of error to reduce and which knobs are allowed to move. It connects to learning from examples, because the hope is that pretrained visual knowledge can be reused rather than relearned. It connects more lightly to systems work, because memory, computation, and prediction-time cost are not secondary details; they decide whether an approach can run in many real settings. The survey's theme, parameter-efficient vision transformers, is therefore a specific version of a recurring 2026 problem: how to reuse a large general model while paying only for the small part that a new task actually needs.
ww: The approach works as a survey because the methods it organizes all exploit the same structure in the world: many image tasks share visual building blocks. A model pretrained on massive image data has already learned useful ways to separate edges, textures, parts, shapes, and object-level patterns, even if the abstract does not enumerate those exact features. For a new classification task, the whole visual understanding system often does not need to be rewritten. It needs steering. Parameter-efficient methods work when the new task can be handled by small adjustments to how existing visual evidence is routed, combined, or read out. Additive pieces can carry task-specific corrections while leaving the original model stable. Compact update recipes can capture common directions of change without storing a full new model. Selective training works if the chosen parts are where task-specific decisions concentrate. The taxonomy helps because it explains why different methods succeed for different reasons. It prevents a false comparison where all efficient fine-tuning is treated as the same. Instead, it asks which resource is being saved, where adaptability is preserved, and where the method may have paid for efficiency by giving up expressive room.
po: The payoff is a clearer decision map for deploying vision transformers on image classification tasks. The survey gathers parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches into additive-based, reparameterization-based, selective, hybrid, and inference-efficient categories, then analyzes their design principles, strengths, limitations, evaluation protocols, reported results, and tradeoffs. That buys researchers and practitioners a way to reason about method choice without treating efficiency as one vague promise. The practical capability is cheaper adaptation of pretrained vision models across diverse downstream tasks while preserving much of the benefit of large-scale pretraining. The paper also identifies open challenges and future directions for making these methods more reliable, efficient, and deployable.
limits: The abstract describes a survey, so its claims are organizational and analytical rather than a new empirical guarantee for one method. The usefulness of the taxonomy depends on whether the reviewed methods are compared under evaluation protocols that are fair enough to reveal real tradeoffs. Parameter-efficient tuning assumes the pretrained vision transformer already contains reusable visual knowledge for the downstream task; if the new task is too different, changing only a small subset of parameters may be insufficient. Efficiency also has several meanings. Saving training memory does not automatically save prediction-time cost, and preserving accuracy on common image classification evaluations does not prove reliability across all deployment settings. The abstract names open challenges but does not prove that they are solved.
